SIKHISM - THE WAY OF THE GURUS

OPENING TEXT: THE MOOL MANTRA
- The chapter opens with the Mool Mantra from the Granth Sahib (the Sikh holy book).
- It says God is one, the first, and all that is. His name is Truth. He is the Creator of all.
- God fears nothing and strikes fear in nothing. His form is eternity. He is the one self-existent.
- Sikhs are told to "continually repeat his name" through the grace of his true servant.
- God "was in the beginning", is "through all ages" and "shall be the one who lives forever".
- Key idea: Sikhism believes in ONE God who is eternal, true and the Creator.

KEY TERMS (ONE-LINE DEFINITIONS)
- Sikh: a follower or disciple (the meaning of the word "Sikh").
- Guru: a teacher; Sikhism had ten human gurus, then the holy book became the Guru.
- Granth Sahib (also called Guru Granth Sahib or Adi Sahib): the Sikh book of scriptures, which became the permanent Guru.
- Mool Mantra: the opening statement of belief about God in the Granth Sahib.
- Mystic contemplation: meditating on God and the name of God; one of the two basic features of Sikhism.
- Social awareness: active involvement in daily life and service of others; the second basic feature of Sikhism.
- Seva: service to others (physical, mental and material) without expecting any reward; seen as a true form of worship.
- Nam kapna: to bring God to mind (first key duty).
- Kirat karna: to work honestly (second key duty).
- Vand chhakna: to practise charity (third key duty).
- Maya: delusion; all people are under its power and cannot think or understand clearly.
- Sahaj: union with God, the goal of salvation; may take many reincarnations.
- Haumai: self-centred pride, which is destroyed by the spiritual pilgrimage.
- Khalsa: the "Brotherhood of the Pure", a community of adult Sikh men and women set up by Guru Gobind Singh in 1699.
- Amrita: sacred sugar-water, the "nectar of immortality", used in the initiation (baptism) ceremony.
- Singh: means "lion"; the name given to Khalsa men to show strength and discipline.
- Kaur: means "princess"; the name given to Khalsa women.
- The five Ks: five signs of faith worn by Khalsa members.
- Panj-Piaras: the five "beloved pure ones" - the first five volunteers of the Khalsa.
- Gurdwara: a Sikh temple.
- Langar: the kitchen in every gurdwara, where communal meals are prepared and shared.
- Sangat: the community of members, where all are equal.
- Ardas: an important prayer that remembers those martyred for their religion.
- Gurpurbs: the five major anniversary ceremonies.
- Melas: annual fairs or large community rituals, following a lunar calendar.

ORIGINS: GURU NANAK (1469-1539)
- Guru Nanak was the first of ten gurus (teachers). His followers are called Sikhs (followers/disciples).
- He was born of Hindu parents near Lahore in the Punjab region of Northern India.
- From an early age he took a deep interest in both Hindu and Muslim teaching and practice.
- He wandered around India in search of truth and wisdom.
- At about 38 years old he had a religious experience in the form of a vision: God had chosen him to proclaim the true name of God.
- He announced: "I am neither a Hindu nor a Muslim" and offered people an alternative way of life.
- His teachings of SERVICE, MEDITATION and HUMILITY became the foundation of Sikhism.

GURU NANAK'S TEACHING ABOUT GOD
- God transcends (goes beyond) all religious manifestations and distinctions.
- What matters most is to allow God's grace to be experienced through worship and meditation.
- This gave Sikhism a strong mystical root: followers meditate on the name of God through sacred hymns.
- He spent much time in dialogue with Muslims and Hindus, while his followers developed their own identity and prayer practice.
- He rejected the idea that any prophet, god, race or religion is exclusive or unique.
- He taught that the universe is God's creation and lives according to God's will.
- Religion is a search for this ultimate reality and a means towards achieving harmony with God.
- Quote: "O my mind. Thou art a spark of the Supreme Light. Know thy essence."
- Guru Nanak rejected the ascetic or monastic life as a path to spiritual growth. He married and had a family; his followers work together as families. God is found in one's relationship with others, and Sikhs see no spiritual benefit in remaining single.

THE TEN GURUS AND THE GRANTH SAHIB
- Guru Nanak was followed by nine other gurus over the next 150 years.
- Each shaped the religion institutionally, socially, politically and religiously, adding his own wisdom and strength.
- They guided the community on its spiritual journey but were NEVER thought of as manifestations (forms) of God. God is the ultimate and true Guru.
- They were simply holy men chosen for their worthiness and spiritual insights.
- The ten gurus in the chapter's picture: Guru Nanak (first) and Guru Gobind Singh (tenth, final), plus Guru Angad, Guru Amar Das, Guru Ram Das, Guru Arjan, Guru Hargobind, Guru Har Rai, Guru Hari Krishan and Guru Tegh Bahadur.
- The tenth and last guru, Gobind Singh (1666-1708), declared that the book of scriptures, the Granth Sahib, should become the Guru for the Sikhs. The cycle of human gurus was completed.
- The Granth Sahib is a book of spiritual poetry written by the historical gurus.
- It is the permanent focus and basis for worship and a central feature of every Sikh ritual.
- It contains 5,894 hymns. Guru Nanak contributed 974. Others came from Hindu and Muslim religious thinkers.
- It is not a systematic explanation of belief and practice but "a poetic inspiration for the heart to love God".

BASIC FEATURES AND VALUES OF SIKHISM
- Two basic features: (1) mystic contemplation of God; (2) social awareness and active participation in daily life.
- Sikhism is a way of life that emphasises practical goodness.
- Five qualities a Sikh should develop: love of God, self-control, forgiveness, contentment, humility.
- Seva: service to others, physical, mental and material, without expecting material reward. It is a true form of worship.
- The three key duties:
- 1. Nam kapna - bring God to mind.
- 2. Kirat karna - work honestly.
- 3. Vand chhakna - practise charity.

CHARACTER, SALVATION AND REINCARNATION
- Character-building is central in Sikhism.
- Sikhs aim to control the five main vices: anger, greed, false pride, lust, attachment to worldly things.
- All people are under the power of maya (delusion) and cannot think or understand clearly.
- Salvation lies in union with God, which comes through worship, service and humility.
- This union is called sahaj. It may take many reincarnations.
- True service to God and to other people is central to all lives.
- When a person finds the true Guru, through God's grace (and only a few do), the transmigration of the soul (rebirth) ends.
- The spiritual pilgrimage is NOT travelling to sacred sites. It means moving the focus from self to God.
- This destroys haumai (self-centred pride) and allows the soul true union with God.
- Motto linked with Sikhism: "He who conquers his mind conquers the world."

THE KHALSA (BROTHERHOOD OF THE PURE)
- Founded by Guru Gobind Singh, the last of the ten gurus, in 1699.
- A community of adult Sikh men and women who promise to uphold Sikh religious values and discipline.
- Initiation is a baptismal ceremony (Amrita) using sacred sugar-water stirred with a sword.
- Men are given the name Singh (lion) to show strength and discipline. Women are called Kaur (princess).
- Sikh symbol: the circle stands for one God without beginning or end; the two outer swords stand for Sikh readiness to defend truth and justice.

THE FIVE Ks
- Kachla: knee-length shorts, expressing discipline and readiness.
- Kirpan: a sword, for a spiritual warrior.
- Kesh: uncut hair, symbolising dedication.
- Kangha: a comb for the hair, maintaining cleanliness.
- Kara: a metal bangle, signifying belonging and obedience.
- The five Ks recall the five volunteers who came forward when Guru Gobind Singh asked for human sacrifices. Instead of being killed, they were presented as his beloved pure ones, powerful in defending the faith and strong in building a moral society. They are called the Panj-Piaras.
- The number five is important in Sikhism (five Ks, five Panj-Piaras, five vices, five qualities, five prayers and five handfuls of amrita at initiation, five gurpurbs).

NUMBERS AND WHERE SIKHS LIVE
- About twenty million Sikhs in the world today.
- About 80 per cent live in the Punjab in north-west India, where the faith began.
- Half a million in Britain; about 225,000 in Canada; about 100,000 in the USA.

THE LIFESTYLE OF BELIEVERS: EQUALITY AND COMMUNITY
- All Sikhs are equal.
- There is no ordained priesthood, and no monks or nuns.
- Any suitably educated Sikh may lead community worship in the gurdwara (temple).
- Guru Nanak set up and encouraged communal eating and a tradition of hospitality.
- Every gurdwara has a kitchen (langar) and an eating room where all share communal meals.
- This community of members (Sangat) is very different from the caste system of Hinduism, which Guru Nanak always criticised.
- People of all castes and backgrounds can meditate together.
- Equality and democracy are described as the two outstanding characteristics of Sikhism.

THE FOUR LIFE CEREMONIES
- Four main ceremonies: naming, initiation, marriage, death.
- 1. NAMING: babies are brought to the temple. A random reading from the Guru Granth Sahib (also called Adi Sahib) is used as the basis for choosing the name.
- 2. INITIATION: for young Sikhs aged between eight and fifteen.
- Performed by five baptised Sikhs, who prepare the amrita (nectar of immortality) and recite five prayers.
- Candidates bathe, carry the five marks of the Khalsa, drink five handfuls of amrita and are sprinkled five times with the holy nectar.
- They are now full members of the Sikh community and accept its responsibilities and obligations.
- 3. MARRIAGE: Guru Amar Das described marriage as becoming "one spirit within two bodies".
- The ceremony centres on the Guru Granth Sahib.
- The bride follows the groom around (the book) four times, while four verses of the marriage hymn are sung. The hymn was composed by Guru Ram Das. These songs are about duty, obligation and love.
- 4. DEATH: cremation, with a short service of suitable hymns.
- The body is washed with water and yogurt to purify it, dressed in the five Ks and cremated.
- Memorials such as gravestones are discouraged, because the body is an empty shell without the soul.
- Afterwards there is continuous reading of the Guru Granth Sahib at home or in the gurdwara for seven to ten days.

DAILY PRAYER
- Sikhs ritually bathe and meditate each morning, with more hymns and prayers before evening.
- Every Sikh is expected to set aside a room, or part of a room, to revere a copy of the Guru Granth Sahib with ritual movements and prayers.
- The Ardas is an important prayer. It remembers those martyred for their religion.
- Sikhs also pray for the welfare of all and for the unity of their community.
- The Ardas ends: "May the whole world be blessed by your grace."

GURPURBS (FIVE MAJOR ANNIVERSARIES)
- Sikhs mark the anniversaries of the birth and death of the ten human gurus. Five are major ceremonies called gurpurbs:
- Guru Nanak's birthday.
- Guru Gobind Singh's birthday.
- Guru Arjan Dev's martyrdom.
- Guru Tegh Bahadur's martyrdom.
- The birthday of the Khalsa.
- Each is preceded by forty-eight hours of continuous reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, then community feasting.

MELAS (ANNUAL FAIRS), FOLLOWING A LUNAR CALENDAR
- BAISAKHI: New Year's Day, a spring festival commemorating the founding of the Khalsa. Colourful processions through the streets of Amritsar, led by five Sikhs in traditional costume representing the first five members of the Khalsa. The Guru Granth Sahib is carried in procession, hymns are sung, and there is a special ceremony to renew commitment to the faith.
- DIVALI: the Festival of Light, common to Hindus and Sikhs.
- HOLA MOHALLA: commemorates Sikh battles. Carnival atmosphere, with military parades, archery contests and martial arts displays.

THE GOLDEN TEMPLE AT AMRITSAR (FROM THE ASSIGNMENTS)
- Surrounded by the "Pool of Nectar". It has four doors.
- The Akal Takht is a political and community centre.
- The building is an example of the unity of Sikh religion and social life.

SIKHISM TODAY
- Sikhism focuses on the community and a deeply spiritual and moral life, which brings honour to the Khalsa and leads to union with God.
- It is NOT a missionary religion. It does not try to gain converts; it seeks to keep its own community intact.
- It does not deny the truth of other faiths and does not feel it must convert people. Its main concern is the community of the faithful and their spiritual journey.
- For Sikhs, membership of the religion and of the community go hand in hand. The development of Punjab's identity was deeply linked with the rise of Sikhism.

PERSECUTION AND CONFLICT
- The one major tradition Sikhs liaise with is Hinduism, but this is more a political dialogue than a religious one.
- 1947: at the partition of India, much of the Punjab was made part of Muslim Pakistan. Over half a million Sikhs died in the fighting. After centuries of persecution this was "the final betrayal" and left Sikhs very alienated.
- 1970: after years of Sikh demands, a Sikh-dominated state was set up in Punjab. Sikh separation is still a troubled issue.
- 1984 and 1988: the Golden Temple of Amritsar saw violence between Sikh extremists and the Indian army.
- June 1984: the invasion of the sacred temple led directly to the assassination of Prime Minister Indira Gandhi in October 1984. This caused more riots in which thousands of Sikhs died.
- Today the rise of Hindu nationalism has increased Sikh fear of persecution.
- Sign of hope: 1999, positive coverage by the Indian and world press of the 300th anniversary of the Sikh Khalsa. Such attitudes are "the way forward to dialogue and acceptance".
- Sikhs respect the truth of other faiths but have not been treated in the same way in return (not reciprocally), and this prevents dialogue.
- 1969: the Sikh Missionary Society was founded in England and the Sikh Research Centre in Canada. These gave Sikhs recognition as distinctive communities, and their self-awareness and confidence has continued to grow.

CHAPTER KEY TERMS LIST
- Gurus, Granth Sahib, Mystic contemplation, Social awareness, Khalsa, The five Ks, Gurdwara, Langar, Sangat, Amrita.

rows.prompt: Explain why the Granth Sahib is called the Guru by Sikhs today.

The Granth Sahib, written by the historical gurus with hymns from Hindu and Muslim thinkers, is now the permanent focus of worship and central to every Sikh ritual.

rows.prompt: Name and explain the three key duties of a Sikh.

rows.prompt: Explain in your own words what Sikhs believe about salvation.

rows.prompt: Name the five Ks and say what each one symbolises.

rows.prompt: Describe what happens at a Sikh funeral.

rows.prompt: Outline two events that caused conflict between Sikhs and others in modern India.

In June 1984 the Indian army invaded the Golden Temple at Amritsar, which led to the assassination of Prime Minister Indira Gandhi in October 1984 and riots in which thousands of Sikhs died.

rows.prompt: Outline the life and teaching of Guru Nanak, the founder of Sikhism.
rows.model_answer: Guru Nanak (1469-1539) was born of Hindu parents near Lahore in the Punjab region of Northern India. From an early age he was deeply interested in both Hindu and Muslim teaching and practice, and he wandered around India searching for truth and wisdom. At about thirty-eight he had a vision in which God chose him to proclaim the true name of God. He announced, 'I am neither a Hindu nor a Muslim', and offered an alternative way of life. His teachings of service, meditation and humility became the foundation of Sikhism. He taught that God transcends all religious distinctions and that people should allow God's grace to be experienced through worship and meditation, especially by meditating on God's name through sacred hymns. He rejected the idea that any prophet, god, race or religion is exclusive or unique. The universe is God's creation and religion is a search for ultimate reality and harmony with God: 'O my mind. Thou art a spark of the Supreme Light. Know thy essence.' He spent much time in dialogue with Hindus and Muslims, criticised the caste system and began the tradition of communal eating. He also rejected the monastic life, marrying and raising a family, because God is found in relationships with others.

rows.prompt: Describe the Khalsa and explain the significance of the five Ks for Sikhs.
rows.model_answer: The Khalsa, the 'Brotherhood of the Pure', was established in 1699 by Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth and last human guru. It is a community of adult Sikh men and women who undertake to uphold Sikh religious values and discipline. Members are initiated in a baptismal ceremony using amrita, sacred sugar-water stirred with a sword. Five baptised Sikhs prepare the amrita and recite five prayers; candidates drink five handfuls and are sprinkled five times. Men take the name Singh (lion) to show strength and discipline and women take the name Kaur (princess). Khalsa members wear the five Ks. The Kachla, knee-length shorts, expresses discipline and readiness. The Kirpan is the sword of a spiritual warrior. Kesh, uncut hair, symbolises dedication. The Kangha, a comb, keeps the hair clean. The Kara, a metal bangle, signifies belonging and obedience. The five Ks recall the Panj-Piaras, the five volunteers who came forward when Guru Gobind Singh asked for human sacrifices and were instead presented as his beloved pure ones, powerful in defending the faith and strong in building a moral society. So the five Ks give Sikhs a visible identity and remind them of courage, commitment and discipline.
rows.marking_scheme: Describe the Khalsa: 8 marks (founder, 1699, community of adult men and women, values and discipline, amrita ceremony, Singh/Kaur - 2 marks per accurate point). Five Ks: 12 marks (name and meaning of each K, plus link to the Panj-Piaras and their significance). Very good answers explain significance, not just list.

rows.prompt: 'Equality and democracy are the two outstanding characteristics of Sikhism.' Discuss this statement with reference to Sikh community life and worship.
rows.model_answer: Sikhism teaches that all Sikhs are equal. There is no ordained priesthood and no monks or nuns, so any suitably educated Sikh, man or woman, may lead community worship in the gurdwara. Even the gurus were not seen as manifestations of God but as holy men chosen for their worthiness, and since Guru Gobind Singh the Granth Sahib itself has been the Guru, so no human holds supreme religious power. Guru Nanak began a tradition of communal eating and hospitality. Every gurdwara has a langar, a kitchen, and an eating room where all share meals together. The Sangat, the community of members, welcomes people of all castes and backgrounds to meditate together, in sharp contrast to the Hindu caste system, which Guru Nanak consistently criticised. The Khalsa is open to both adult men and women, who take the names Singh and Kaur. Values like seva, service without reward, and Vand chhakna, charity, build a caring community. Guru Nanak also rejected the exclusiveness of any race or religion. This equality gives Sikhs strong community relations and a confident identity, which has helped them survive persecution, such as at partition in 1947 and the violence at Amritsar in 1984.
rows.marking_scheme: Very good 16-20, good 10-15, fair 0-9. May refer to: no priesthood/monks/nuns; any educated Sikh leads worship; gurus not divine; Granth Sahib as Guru; langar and communal meals; Sangat open to all castes; criticism of caste; Khalsa open to men and women; seva; charity; rejection of exclusiveness; strong identity and community. Must engage with the statement (discuss), not just describe.

rows.prompt: Describe two rites of passage in Sikhism.
rows.model_answer: Sikhism has four main ceremonies marking life: naming, initiation, marriage and death. Initiation happens for young Sikhs between eight and fifteen. It is a baptismal ceremony performed by five baptised Sikhs, who prepare the amrita, the nectar of immortality, and recite five prayers. The candidates bathe, carry the five marks of the Khalsa, drink five handfuls of amrita and are sprinkled five times with the holy nectar. They are then full members of the Sikh community and accept its responsibilities and obligations. Marriage was described by Guru Amar Das as becoming 'one spirit within two bodies'. The ceremony centres on the Guru Granth Sahib. The bride follows her groom around four times while four verses of the marriage hymn, composed by Guru Ram Das, are sung. Points may include: naming - baby brought to temple, random reading of the Granth chooses name; initiation - age 8-15, five baptised Sikhs, amrita, five prayers, five handfuls, sprinkled five times, full membership; marriage - Guru Amar Das quote, centred on Granth, four circuits, hymn of Guru Ram Das; death - washed with water and yogurt, five Ks, cremation, no gravestones, 7-10 days reading.
